messages.text: Held out of sprint 2026-10-06 (intake drain). We don't understand how requiring process ids for ports wouldn't be a burden on whatever is starting those processes. We don't know all the process types that a project or stack might need to run and don't understand how that approach wouldn't be fragile later. There are a huge number of ports, and we can know if a lease is stuck by grace of the project no longer running any ad hoc stacks. And the implementation should be project local, not a global registry. Each project should be configurable with a range, then allocate ports only there. Unless projects are running a huge number of parallel tests or drivers, a few hundred (or even dozen) ports should suffice.

You are right about option C, and its cost line understated the problem. A process id check is fragile beyond the work of writing it: a server started through a wrapper (an npm script, a shell script, a process manager) reports the wrapper's id, not the listener's; a container's id belongs to another namespace; and the operating system reuses ids, so an unrelated live process can pass. I rewrote C's cost to say so.

Your direction is an option the analysis missed, and I added it as option D with a recommended ruling for it. It works against this issue's harm because the harm needs the operating system to hand a freed port to the next run. Today every stack binds port 0, so the operating system picks from its ephemeral range (49152 to 65535 here) and nothing keeps a freed port away from the next run. Under a project-local lease, a stopped server's port stays leased to its run, so that run's readback hits a port nothing listens on and fails, instead of passing against another run's server. A stuck lease fails safe: it wastes one port until you clear the leases while no stack runs, as you say.

Two points the ruling should settle. First, the current decision's Rationale rejects every allocator because a program outside the scheme can bind a port between the lease and the stack's bind. Placing the range below the ephemeral range narrows that to a program that binds a fixed port in the range, and such a collision fails the stack's bind loudly. Second, a lease store in one checkout is invisible to another checkout of the same project, so concurrent runs from two worktrees would share a range unless the store sits where every worktree reads it, such as the git common directory.

Revised after the owner's comment. problem: added a section, Why the port goes to another run, explaining that the harm depends on the operating system reassigning a freed port and that a project-local lease removes that condition; reframed the closing Options line around OS-assigned ports versus a project-local range; corrected the ADMINISTRATION.md link from line 159 to line 160. options: rewrote A to drop the misplaced claim about allocators; rewrote C's cost to name the fragility the owner raised (wrappers, container namespaces, reused process ids); added D, a project-local port range with leases, with its cost against the decision's Rationale. recommendation: added a recommended ruling for D, with the worktree case as its flip.

options.label: A
options.text: **Probe the port.** Amend [os-assigned-ports-read-back-by-run-tag](.ok-planner/design/decisions/os-assigned-ports-read-back-by-run-tag.md) so that the readback refuses a recorded port nothing listens on. Cost: another run's server may already listen on the freed port, and the probe then passes, so it narrows the hole and cannot close it.

options.label: B
options.text: **Make stack-stop clear records.** Amend [os-assigned-ports-read-back-by-run-tag](.ok-planner/design/decisions/os-assigned-ports-read-back-by-run-tag.md) to state that a readback reports what the record holds, and that the project's stack-stop command deletes the run's records. Cost: the duty moves to every project's stack commands, and a crashed server, which runs no stop command, still leaves a stale record.

options.label: C
options.text: **Record the writer.** Amend [os-assigned-ports-read-back-by-run-tag](.ok-planner/design/decisions/os-assigned-ports-read-back-by-run-tag.md) so that the record holds the server's process id beside the port, and the readback refuses when that process is gone. Cost: every project's dev server must write both values, and the check is fragile. A server started through a wrapper (an npm script, a shell script, a process manager) reports the wrapper's process id, not the listener's. A container's process id belongs to another namespace. The operating system reuses process ids, so an unrelated live process can pass the check.

options.label: D
options.text: **Lease ports from a project-local range.** Replace [os-assigned-ports-read-back-by-run-tag](.ok-planner/design/decisions/os-assigned-ports-read-back-by-run-tag.md) with a decision that a project declares a port range in `.ok-planner/config.json`, and `port-block <run-tag>` leases one port per declared name from that range to the tag and prints them. The stack binds the ports it is given: a dev server reads its port from the environment, and a compose file publishes `${NAME}:<container port>`. The lease store lives in the project, not in a registry shared across projects. A leased port goes to no other tag while its lease stands, and the least recently released port goes out first. The stack-stop command releases its tag's leases, and the owner clears every lease when the project runs no stack. Cost: the decision's Rationale argues that any allocator races, because a program outside the scheme can bind a port between the lease and the stack's bind. A range below the operating system's ephemeral range narrows that race to a program that binds a fixed port in the range, and that collision makes the stack's bind fail loudly. A crashed run leaves its lease stuck, which costs one port of the range until the next clear, and an exhausted range refuses. Two projects whose ranges overlap can collide, so each owner picks a distinct range. The record and service entry forms, the run-tag concept's citation of the decision, the cheatsheet's rule "Never pick a port in one program for another to bind later", and the Ports paragraph of the administration document all change with it.

problem:
`port-block` tells a verification run which host ports its own stack got. It handles two kinds of entry. A service entry names a container. When no container of that service runs, `port-block` refuses. A record entry names a file a dev server wrote its port to. `port-block` prints that port with exit 0 whether or not the server still runs. The story [concurrent-stacks-without-port-collisions](.ok-planner/design/stories/concurrent-stacks-without-port-collisions.md) promises that one verification run never disturbs another's results. A stale record can break that promise.

## How it happens

A dev server listens on port 0, the operating system hands it a free port, and the server writes that port to a file whose path holds the run tag. `port-block <run-tag>` later reads the file back ([`plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/port-block`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/port-block), [`recorded_port`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/port-block#L142-L150)). It refuses only when the file is missing or holds no port number. [`ADMINISTRATION.md`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L160) describes the record entry and says nothing about who removes the file.

The file outlives its server unless something deletes it. A run tag is unique to one run, so a later run never reads an earlier run's file. The harm falls inside one run: its server stops or crashes, the operating system gives the freed port to another run's server, and the first run reads its record back and verifies against the other run's server. The run sees a passing result that belongs to someone else.

Evidence, from drive failure i28 in sprint certification run converge-2026-10-04T060800: after run B's dev server stopped, `port-block run-1d45e73b9246` printed `DB_PORT=55058` and `WEB_PORT=55061` and exited 0, and `curl -s -m 2 localhost:55061` exited 7, connection refused. After run A's compose stack went down, its service entry refused: `no running container of service db in compose project run-7478b68995b5`, exit 1.

## What the corpus says

The decision [os-assigned-ports-read-back-by-run-tag](.ok-planner/design/decisions/os-assigned-ports-read-back-by-run-tag.md) says `port-block` "reads back, by that tag, the host ports the stack got". It also says that where a stack cannot bind this way, "the project's own stack commands handle isolation". The concept [run-tag](.ok-planner/design/concepts/run-tag.md) says wiring the tag into stacks is the project's own change. Neither says what happens to a record whose server has stopped. If the decision promises a live readback, the accept list's entry for a false report someone acts on ([A9](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L17)) covers this, and it is a defect.

## Why the port goes to another run

The harm needs two things: a freed port, and an operating system that hands it to the next server that asks. Under the decision every stack binds port 0, so the operating system picks from its whole ephemeral range (49152 to 65535 on this machine, by `sysctl net.inet.ip.portrange`), and nothing keeps a freed port away from the next run. Options A to C keep port 0 and try to detect the stale record afterward. Option D, the owner's direction, removes the second condition: the project hands out ports from a range it owns, and a port leased to one run goes to no other run until that lease ends. A run whose server has stopped then reads back a port nothing listens on, and its checks fail with connection refused instead of passing against someone else's server.

## Options

The ruling decides whether ports stay OS-assigned with a check on the readback, or come from a project-local range by lease.

recommendation.text:
Option D. Replace [os-assigned-ports-read-back-by-run-tag](.ok-planner/design/decisions/os-assigned-ports-read-back-by-run-tag.md) with a decision that each project declares a port range in `.ok-planner/config.json`, below the operating system's ephemeral range, and that `port-block <run-tag>` leases one port per declared name from that range to the tag, from a lease store the project holds, handing out the least recently released port first. The stack binds the ports it is given. A leased port goes to no other tag until its lease is released: by the stack-stop command, or by the owner's clear of every lease when the project runs no stack. An exhausted range refuses with a message naming the stuck tags. Update the run-tag concept's citation of the decision, the cheatsheet's per-run section, the Ports paragraph of [`ADMINISTRATION.md`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L160), and [`port-block`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/port-block) to match.

Rationale: the owner ruled out process ids as a burden on every kind of process a stack starts, and directed a project-local range. Under a lease, a stopped server's port stays idle, so a stale readback fails with connection refused instead of passing against another run's server, which is what [concurrent-stacks-without-port-collisions](.ok-planner/design/stories/concurrent-stacks-without-port-collisions.md) needs. A stuck lease fails safe: it wastes one port, and a range of a few hundred ports absorbs many crashes before a clear. The race the current decision's Rationale names remains only for a program outside the scheme that binds a fixed port inside the range, and that program makes the stack's bind fail, not pass. The flip case: if the project runs verification from several checkouts at once, each checkout's lease store is separate, so the ruling should either give each checkout its own range or place the store where every worktree of the project reads it, such as the git common directory.

title: port-block prints a dev server's recorded port after that server has stopped

options.label: A
options.text: Record "converge" as an alias of true-up, and say in the concept's Boundaries that the `/converge` command is a different act. Cost: one live word still names two acts, and the template's two-names issue stands at every audit.

options.label: B
options.text: Use "true-up" alone for the administration act in the corpus, the suite's documents, the core and its mode, and the stamp wording, and keep "converge" for the `/converge` defect run. Cost: a rewrite of about 60 corpus sentences, the integration contract, the administration document, and the core, and a new stamp line in every suite-owned file on the next `/ok`.

options.label: C
options.text: Rename the `/converge` command so "converge" names only the administration act. Cost: it renames a slash verb that crosses the release boundary, which every owner and every sprint's closing step (`/converge sprint <path>`) calls.

problem:
The corpus uses "converge" both for the suite's administration act, which [concept:true-up](.ok-planner/design/concepts/true-up.md) defines, and for the `/converge` command, the defect run, a different act. That breaks the concept template's rule that a concept has one live name, and a reader cannot tell from the word alone which act a sentence means.

The mechanism. [concept:true-up](.ok-planner/design/concepts/true-up.md) calls the act "the idempotent converge of a project's suite presence" and says "Which content converge may move or write without asking is the ownership rule's", and it has no Aliases section. [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md) names the act "converge" throughout ("Converge removes a committed one whole", "converge rewrites the line"), and so do [concept:materialized-artifact](.ok-planner/design/concepts/materialized-artifact.md), [concept:estate](.ok-planner/design/concepts/estate.md), and [concept:integration-contract](.ok-planner/design/concepts/integration-contract.md). The front door's core that performs the act is the file [`admin/converge`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge), run in a mode named converge, and the stamp line on every suite-owned file reads "overwritten on converge". The `/converge` skill ([converge](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md)) finds and fixes defects, and about 18 corpus lines name it. The concept template ([artifact-definitions](.claude/skills/_shared/artifact-definitions.md#L69)) says "Two live names for one concept is an issue: file it", and the audit's vocabulary reading of a concept looks for one live name.

The state of play. Readers have told the two acts apart from context so far, and no accept-list entry names the ambiguity as a defect. The `/converge` verb crosses the release boundary to every converged project, because vendored skill names and their slash verbs do. The core's mode name and the stamp wording do not, because the suite rewrites both on the next `/ok`. The compliance review of sprint 2026-10-05-second-intake-drain raised the issue and left it for its own ruling.

The ruling decides which act keeps the word "converge".

recommendation.text:
Name the administration act "true-up" everywhere the suite writes about it: the design corpus, the suite's own documents and rules, the stamp line on suite-owned files, and the core and its mode that perform the act. "Converge" then names only the `/converge` defect run.

Rationale: B is the only option that gives each act one name, which the concept template and the writing standard's "use the same term for the same thing every time" both ask for, without breaking a verb that crosses the release boundary as C does. A records the double name rather than resolving it, so the concept's vocabulary reading keeps failing and the issue returns at each audit. B's reach is wide but mechanical, and everything it touches outside the corpus is suite-owned and rewritten whole on the next `/ok`. Flip case: if the owner judges the rename's reach larger than the harm of an ambiguity readers have so far resolved from context, A is the cheap holding answer, taken knowing the template's issue stays open.

title: "Converge" names two different acts: the true-up and the `/converge` defect run

problem:
Site: [implementation-auditor.md:coverage auditor Method step 1](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/implementation-auditor.md#L499-L504) and [implementation-auditor.md:reading auditor quantifier step](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/implementation-auditor.md#L117-L122), with [audit/SKILL.md:task prompt resolution](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/audit/SKILL.md#L132), which writes those prompts into the run's task bodies and tells them no folder.

Entry: [A8](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L16), through [decision:project-declares-its-folders](.ok-planner/design/decisions/project-declares-its-folders.md): "Every tool that lists or scopes the project's code reads that list." [story:project-spans-folders](.ok-planner/design/stories/project-spans-folders.md) owes the same: "so that no check the suite runs over my project misses code I own."

Trigger: a project declares `folders` in `.ok-planner/config.json` and keeps code that a subject's population or a quantified claim covers in one of those folders.

Harm: the coverage auditor and the reading auditor enumerate a population from the project root alone, so a member under a declared folder is never counted, and a practice violation there is never filed. The audit's `checked:` count then reports coverage it did not measure.

Evidence: [implementation-auditor.md#L501](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/implementation-auditor.md#L501) says only "Enumerate from the codebase", and [implementation-auditor.md#L118](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/implementation-auditor.md#L118) only "enumerate the population from reality". A search for `folders` under plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills hits only [converge/SKILL.md#L36](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L36), [converge/SKILL.md#L53](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L53), [audit/SKILL.md#L99](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/audit/SKILL.md#L99) (the surface extractor), and [audit/SKILL.md#L204](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/audit/SKILL.md#L204) (the lint sweep). The auditor prompts never read the list.

A merge agent confirmed it in run converge-2026-10-06T034157 (drive failure i8). The files stand unchanged since base 1ff2a91, so the defect lies outside sprint 2026-10-05-second-intake-drain.

recommendation.text: Fix [plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/implementation-auditor.md:coverage auditor Method step 1](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/implementation-auditor.md#L499-L504) and [reading auditor quantifier step](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/implementation-auditor.md#L117-L122), and [plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/audit/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/audit/SKILL.md#L132) where it resolves those prompts, so the auditors enumerate each folder `.ok-planner/config.json` declares under `folders` and no population member under a declared folder goes uncounted.

title: The audit's coverage and reading auditors never learn the folders the project declares beside its root

problem:
Sites: [converge:strip_story_sections](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3069-L3086) and [converge:strip_decision_proofs](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3089-L3099), which the core's `corpus` mode runs on every `/ok` with no question. [ADMINISTRATION.md#L201](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L201) and [ADMINISTRATION.md#L371](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L371) describe the same behavior.

Entries: [A2](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L10), a delete or an overwrite reaches something it should not: cleanup reaches an owner's untracked concept file the suite did not create, and owner text git holds no copy of. [A8](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L16), through [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md): the machinery "never edits a file a human also edits, save the one removal of a retired family's unread state file and the rewrites of references to retired suite paths", and even that removal sends "an uncommitted or symlinked one ... to the owner like any other estate edit". [story:converge-project-estate](.ok-planner/design/stories/converge-project-estate.md) owes the owner "that upgrading the suite never costs me work I wrote."

Trigger: an owner holds uncommitted or untracked text in a story's `## Falsifier`, `## Proof`, or `## Acceptance` section or a decision's `## Proof` section, or keeps an untracked concept of their own at `design/concepts/falsifier.md`, and runs `/ok`.

Harm: the strip deletes the section text and collapses blank-line runs across the whole file, and the core removes the concept file, with no check of git status. Text git cannot recover is lost.

Evidence: [converge#L3073](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3073) `new = re.sub(r"\n## (Falsifier|Proof|Acceptance)\n.*?(?=\n## |\Z)", "\n", text, flags=re.S)`, [converge#L3074](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3074) `new = re.sub(r"\n{3,}", "\n\n", new)`, [converge#L3080-L3081](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3080-L3081) `if os.path.exists(concept):` then `os.remove(concept)`, and [converge#L3093](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3093) for decisions; neither function reads git. In the drive of the story, the driver's untracked `use-go.md` lost its Proof prose, and its untracked `concepts/falsifier.md` was removed ("Retired story sections eliminated: removed: concepts/falsifier.md").

A merge agent confirmed it in run converge-2026-10-06T034157 (drive failures i9 and i10, one defect). Both functions are byte-identical to base 1ff2a91, so the defect lies outside sprint 2026-10-05-second-intake-drain.

recommendation.text: Fix [plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge:strip_story_sections](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3069-L3086) and [:strip_decision_proofs](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3089-L3099), with the matching text in [plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L201), so an uncommitted, untracked, or symlinked story, decision, or falsifier concept goes to the owner as an estate edit offer and no owner text git cannot recover is rewritten or removed.

title: Converge strips uncommitted story and decision text, and removes an owner's falsifier concept, beyond recovery

problem:
Site: [ADMINISTRATION.md:"Audit the project against the carried version"](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L238-L260), the `.claude/settings.json` row of the "What it reads" table.

Entry: [A9](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L17), the system reports something false that someone acts on.

Trigger: a `.claude/settings.json` hook entry whose command calls a script the carried version materializes under `.ok-planner/bin/`, such as `.ok-planner/bin/run-tag` or `.ok-planner/bin/plumbline`. The converge core writes such an entry itself when it repoints a hook that named a retired script: [ADMINISTRATION.md:"Callers of retired suite scripts"](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L228) names `.ok-planner/bin/plumbline`, `.ok-planner/bin/catalog-toc`, and `.ok-planner/bin/run-tag` as the drop-ins it repoints to.

Harm: the audit's report line tells the owner that a working hook names something the carried version replaced, and the owner acts on it by rewording a valid hook. The report line also leaves the finding pending, so `/ok`'s outcome does not read `converged` on a project that is converged.

Evidence: [ADMINISTRATION.md:249](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L249) makes a finding of "an entry whose command names a path under `.ok-planner/`, `.claude/hooks/`, `.ok-plumbline/`, or `.ok-workspaces/` that the table does not list and the `lint` group's command does not remove", and the wiring table it reads against ([ADMINISTRATION.md:44-49](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L44-L49)) lists only the hook scripts, never `bin/`. [ADMINISTRATION.md:258](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L258) sorts a `.claude/settings.json` entry outside the wiring table as a report line the owner rewords, and [ADMINISTRATION.md:260](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L260) says a report line leaves its finding pending and "`/ok`'s outcome reads `converged` only when none is pending". The executables the core materializes, `bin/run-tag` and `bin/plumbline` among them, are listed at [ADMINISTRATION.md:28](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L28).

A fixer noticed this in run converge-2026-10-06T034157 (call i44); triage re-verified it against the document as it stands.

recommendation.text: Fix [ADMINISTRATION.md:"Audit the project against the carried version"](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L249) so a `.claude/settings.json` hook entry naming a path the carried version still materializes is no finding, and the audit no longer reports a valid hook as a line to reword.

title: The front door's project audit tells the owner to reword a settings hook that calls a live estate script

options.label: A
options.text: The dashboard drive builds the page from the tree's source into a scratch folder outside the tree, places it in the scratch project's dashboard folder, and stamps the version as converge does. Cost: every dashboard drive needs node, npm, and an `npm ci`, and the drive commands repeat the release's build steps and converge's stamp.

options.label: B
options.text: A sprint that changes the page source rebuilds and commits the page build in the same stage. Cost: it reverses [decision:pinned-build-placed-at-converge](.ok-planner/design/decisions/pinned-build-placed-at-converge.md)'s build once per release, so it needs a corpus delta, and every such sprint commits a regenerated bundle.

options.label: C
options.text: The drive commands say a dashboard drive checks page behavior through the JSON routes, the command line, and the page source whenever the sprint changed the page source. Cost: no drive exercises the sprint's real page before a release ships it.

options.label: D
options.text: The drive commands skip the page and record an environment failure for every page check when the page source differs from the source the committed build came from. Cost: the same lost coverage as C; the merge agent only sorts the gap as environment rather than product.

problem:
Sprint certification's dashboard drive serves the page build the last release committed, so a sprint that changes the page source is driven against the old page and fails on a change no fixer can act on. That defeats the drive's job under [decision:drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user.md): to try each story the sprint adds or amends on the running product.

The mechanism. The drive commands in [.ok-planner/review/project.md](.ok-planner/review/project.md#L43) build a scratch project by running the converge core. The core copies the committed bundle at `browser/dist/` into the scratch project's `.ok-planner/dashboard/` ([converge:BUILD_SRC](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L252-L253)) and stamps the suite version into it. Only the release skill's step 5a ([.claude/skills/release/SKILL.md](.claude/skills/release/SKILL.md#L129-L149)) runs `npm ci` and `npm run build`, as [decision:pinned-build-placed-at-converge](.ok-planner/design/decisions/pinned-build-placed-at-converge.md) requires: the page is built once per suite release and carried as payload. Between releases, `browser/src/` moves and `browser/dist/` does not. Today `browser/dist/` last changed at release v25.3.0 (1ff2a91), while the staged sprint changes [`browser/src/lib/api.js`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/lib/api.js), [`browser/src/lib/markdown.js`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/lib/markdown.js), and [`browser/src/views/IssueDetail.svelte`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/views/IssueDetail.svelte).

The state of play. In run converge-2026-10-06T034157, the driver of [story:see-new-analysis](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-new-analysis.md) drove the pre-sprint page and failed. The merge agent read the page source instead and found it right, so the run spent a drive on a failure with nothing to fix. A driver writes nothing in the project tree, so it cannot rebuild `browser/dist/` itself; it may write in a scratch project. The corpus says nothing about how a drive obtains a page build.

The ruling decides where a dashboard drive gets the page it drives when the tree's page source is newer than the committed build.

recommendation.text:
A dashboard drive builds the page from the tree's source into scratch space outside the tree, and the scratch project serves that build in place of the committed release build, stamped with the suite version the way converge stamps the placed build. The drive then certifies the page the sprint changed, and the committed build stays a release artifact.

Rationale: A is the one option that drives the sprint's real page and keeps both standing decisions. [decision:pinned-build-placed-at-converge](.ok-planner/design/decisions/pinned-build-placed-at-converge.md) keeps its build once per release, because the drive's build lives and dies in scratch space. [decision:drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user.md) keeps its rule that a driver writes nothing in the project tree. B reverses the first decision to serve a test need and commits a churning bundle with every page sprint. C and D give up the page coverage certification exists to provide; D only relabels the failure. The repeated build steps are a few commands in the owner's drive facts, a small price for a drive that sees what will ship. Flip case: if the machines that run certification cannot count on node and network access for `npm ci`, a build-from-source drive fails on environment every time, and D becomes the better call, since it names the gap without spending a fixer.

title: A dashboard drive serves the last release's page build, not the page source a sprint changed

options.label: A
options.text: The corpus commits that the readable `issues show` prints each update message's difference, so a session shows the owner the change. Cost: a corpus delta and a change to the readable printer, and long revised fields lengthen the output unless it prints a word diff as the dashboard does.

options.label: B
options.text: The corpus commits that the dashboard and `show --json` are the owner's ways to read an update's difference, and the readable `show` names the revised fields only. Cost: a session walking an issue shows no difference unless the agent reads the JSON.

options.label: C
options.text: The readable `show` prints the difference with no corpus delta, reading "the owner reads the difference" as binding every surface the owner reads. Cost: the change rests on a reading of the decision the owner has not confirmed.

problem:
`.ok-planner/bin/issues show <id>` prints an agent's update message as a head line naming the revised fields and one line of text, and leaves out the before and after text the record holds. [decision:agent-revisions-reach-the-owner](.ok-planner/design/decisions/agent-revisions-reach-the-owner.md) commits that the update message holds each revised field's text before and after, "and the owner reads the difference", but names no place where the owner reads it.

The mechanism. [issues:update_message](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L686-L691) stores a diff of each revised field, before and after, on every update message. [issues:message_line](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L1066-L1076) prints the readable discussion and never reads that diff. [issues:cmd_show](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L1205-L1210) prints the diff only under `--json`. The dashboard draws it as a word diff ([IssueDetail.svelte](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/views/IssueDetail.svelte#L254-L266)). So the owner sees the difference on the dashboard and does not see it in a session. A session is where [decision:flagged-issues-discussed-in-session](.ok-planner/design/decisions/flagged-issues-discussed-in-session.md) has the owner talk an issue over, and where the `/plan-sprint` issue walk ([plan-sprint](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/SKILL.md#L132)) presents each issue through `issues show`. There the owner reads that a field changed, not how.

The state of play. The record holds the difference, and the dashboard shows it. [story:see-new-analysis](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-new-analysis.md) asks only for "a way" to see new revisions, which the dashboard gives. Only the readable `show` leaves the difference out, and it did so before the latest sprint too. No accept-list entry names this as a defect.

The ruling decides whether the readable `issues show` owes the owner the difference, or whether the dashboard and `show --json` are the owner's ways to read it.

recommendation.text:
The readable `issues show` prints each update message's difference, field by field, as a word diff in the shape the dashboard draws. The corpus records that every surface that shows the owner an update message shows its difference.

Rationale: [decision:agent-revisions-reach-the-owner](.ok-planner/design/decisions/agent-revisions-reach-the-owner.md) chose a diff so the owner never rereads a whole field to find an edit, and a session is one of the places the owner reads: [decision:flagged-issues-discussed-in-session](.ok-planner/design/decisions/flagged-issues-discussed-in-session.md) puts discussion there, and the plan-sprint issue walk presents every issue through `show`. B keeps the decision's promise on one surface and breaks it on the one sessions use. C makes the same code change but leaves the decision silent on surfaces, so the next reader faces the same question; the corpus delta makes the promise checkable. Flip case: if the owner reads analysis only on the dashboard and uses sessions only to give rulings, the extra output is noise, and B is the better call.

title: `issues show` names the fields an agent revised but not how they changed

options.label: A
options.text: Name discover-design's `_discover/` scaffolding a record, so converge never repoints a line in it. Cost: a `_discover/` line that does call a retired script is never repointed, and once nothing else names that script, converge removes it and the line points at nothing.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the repoint over every tracked line outside a record, `_discover/` notes included, and leave the owner to reword a line that should keep the retired path. Cost: converge rewrites observation notes to describe a layout the discovery run never saw, naming them only in its report.

options.label: C
options.text: Name `_discover/` a record, and also have converge leave any line that describes a retired path rather than calling it. Cost: converge must judge prose, which a pattern match cannot do, so it needs a marker or a list the owner keeps.

problem:
The converge core rewrites every tracked line outside a record that names a retired suite script's path, and it treats discover-design's `_discover/` notes as corpus rather than record, so it rewrites notes that record what a discovery run observed. [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md) exempts records from the repoint because "A record states what was true when it was written", but the corpus never says whether `_discover/` notes are records.

The mechanism. [converge:repoint_callers](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1804) rewrites a line wherever [converge:script_pattern](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1656) matches a retired script path. [converge:caller_kind](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1691) skips only a file that [review:OWNER_PATHS](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L45-L62) classes as record or suite, plus the rules file and the memory file. OWNER_PATHS classes all of `.ok-planner/design/` as corpus, `_discover/` included. The repoint cannot tell a line that calls a script from a line that describes one. In this repository the next `/ok` would rewrite [_discover/script-materialization.md](.ok-planner/design/_discover/script-materialization.md#L12), which describes the retired lint at its old path, to name the current copy. It would also file an intake issue for [_discover/src-tag.md](.ok-planner/design/_discover/src-tag.md#L14), whose retired script has no drop-in, and keep that retired copy while the note names it.

The state of play. The `_discover/` notes describe the past by their own account: discover-design calls them "the trail of what was observed" ([discover-design](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/discover-design/SKILL.md#L35)), and the current-state-only rule exempts them as point-in-time. The cheatsheet's list of records names `sprints/`, `sketches/`, `documentation/`, and `history/`, and not `_discover/`. The filed concern about migration documentation no longer holds: the administration document names the retired estates only as directories, which the repoint does not match, and no document in the tree names a full retired script path. A sibling issue, retired-script-reference-root-prefix-unsettled, asks about the same repoint's scope for a path behind a root prefix.

The ruling decides whether `_discover/` notes are records the repoint leaves as written.

recommendation.text:
Discover-design's `_discover/` scaffolding is a record: converge leaves its lines as written and does not count them as callers when it decides whether a retired script may go. Everywhere else the repoint stands as decided.

Rationale: [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md) already exempts records because rewriting what was true when written destroys what the text is for, and the `_discover/` notes are that kind of text by their own account and by the current-state-only rule's exemption. A applies the decision's own reason to the notes. B keeps a rewrite that falsifies them. C adds a prose-judging mechanism for a case the tree does not show today, since no document outside `_discover/` names a full retired script path. Flip case: if documents outside `_discover/` begin naming full retired script paths to describe a migration, C's line-level judgment earns its marker.

title: Converge's retired-script repoint rewrites discover-design's observation notes

options.label: A
options.text: The corpus commits that such a message shows in agent styling under its raw author, with no "new" tag, as built. Cost: a malformed message looks like an agent's at a glance.

options.label: B
options.text: The corpus commits that such a message shows under a third style labelled as from an unknown author, neither the owner's nor an agent's. Cost: one more display branch to build and keep.

options.label: C
options.text: The corpus commits that only a known agent's message shows in agent styling, and every other message shows as the owner's. Cost: an unknown author's message is labelled "you" and "not yet seen by triage", a false status.

problem:
The issue dashboard shows every discussion message the owner did not write as an agent's message, and no corpus artifact says how a message from an author who is neither the owner nor a known agent should appear. [decision:agent-revisions-reach-the-owner](.ok-planner/design/decisions/agent-revisions-reach-the-owner.md) and [story:see-new-analysis](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-new-analysis.md) cover agent messages reaching the owner as unread; neither covers a message whose author is unknown.

The mechanism. The intake module checks a message's author only when it writes the message ([issues:one_message_defects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L177)): a comment or ruling must come from `owner`, a reply or update from `triage-issues` or `converge`. On read, [decision:intake-reads-past-stray-lines](.ok-planner/design/decisions/intake-reads-past-stray-lines.md) keeps a record whose old message breaks the schema, and [issues:readable_message](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L295-L301) turns a missing or non-text author into an empty one. So a hand-edited message, or one written by an earlier layout, can reach the dashboard with any author. Only such a message is affected. The dashboard's [api.js:isAgent](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/lib/api.js#L81) reads `message.by !== OWNER`, so [IssueDetail.svelte](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/views/IssueDetail.svelte#L223-L241) shows the message in agent styling under its raw author. Every message that branch rejects shows as "you" with a "not yet seen by triage" or "seen by triage" tag. [api.js:isNew](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/lib/api.js#L76) gives the "new" tag only to an unread message from `triage-issues` or `converge`, matching what the module counts as unread ([issues:unread](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L473)) and marks read ([issues:mark_read](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L921)). The unknown-author message therefore never carries a "new" tag the owner could not clear.

The state of play. As built, the page states nothing false about such a message: it names the raw author and claims no unread status. Its styling alone suggests an agent wrote it. The sprint's implementation notes asked to narrow isAgent to the two agent authors as well; that would move the message to the owner's branch, labelled "you" and "not yet seen by triage", a false status the owner may act on ([accept-list](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md) entry A9's kind of harm). The build kept isAgent as it stands.

The ruling decides how the dashboard shows a message whose author is neither the owner nor a known agent.

recommendation.text:
The dashboard shows a message whose author is neither the owner nor a known agent in agent styling, under its raw author, with no "new" tag. Only a known agent's unread message counts as new.

Rationale: this is option A, the build as it stands. It reports nothing false: the raw author is shown, and no unread state is claimed that the owner could not clear. Option C labels another author's words as the owner's, the false-status harm the accept list names. Option B is honest too, but adds a display branch for a message the intake module never writes and only a hand edit or an earlier layout produces; the project prefers one plain path over a branch for a case its own writer forbids. The flip case: if an earlier layout's conversion or another tool is found to produce such messages in numbers, the owner would need to tell them apart from agent analysis, and option B becomes worth its branch.

title: The dashboard shows a message from an unknown author as an agent's message

options.label: A
options.text: The corpus commits to the built rule: converge repoints a reference only where its prefix certainly names the project root, files an intake issue and keeps the retired copy for a reference whose prefix may name it, and does not see a path built in code. Cost: a retired copy can stay indefinitely until the owner edits the line, and a code-built caller still breaks when the copy goes.

options.label: B
options.text: The corpus commits that converge repoints every reference whose prefix may name the project root, and names each rewrite in its report. Cost: a line about a home or sibling-repository script can be rewritten wrongly, with only a report line as warning.

options.label: C
options.text: The corpus commits that converge leaves an uncertain reference unrewritten, removes the retired copy anyway, and names the line in its report. Cost: a real caller fails at its next run.

options.label: D
options.text: The corpus commits to the rule in A, and also counts as certain a prefix converge can prove resolves to the project root, such as git's top-level idiom where the root is the repository's top. Cost: converge must check that proof on each run, and one more recognized form to maintain.

problem:
When converge migrates a project off a retired suite script, it cannot always tell from a line's text whether the line names the project's retired copy, and the corpus does not say what counts as naming it. [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md) commits converge to rewrite a line in a tracked project file that names a retired suite script's path, and to remove the retired script once no tracked file other than a record names it. It is silent on a line whose path may or may not start at the project root.

The mechanism. A retired script sits either under a retired estate directory (`.ok-plumbline/`, `.ok-workspaces/`, `.ok-review/`, listed in [converge:RETIRED_TOPS](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1614)) or at a project path such as `bin/run-tag`. An estate directory's name belongs to the suite alone, so [converge:script_pattern](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1656-L1663) repoints it behind any prefix. A project path like `bin/run-tag` is common, so converge treats it as certainly the project's copy only behind a line start, `./`, the root's absolute path, or `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/` in its braced and quoted forms ([converge:ROOT_REFERENCES](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1617-L1618)). Behind any other prefix that may resolve to the root, such as `$ROOT/bin/run-tag`, `$HOME/bin/run-tag`, `~/bin/run-tag`, `../bin/run-tag`, or `$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/bin/run-tag`, [converge:may_name_root](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1666-L1675) and [converge:unsure_reference](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1678-L1683) mark the reference unsure. Converge then leaves the line as written, files an intake issue for the owner, and keeps the retired copy. A prefix that cannot be the root, such as `/usr/local/`, is ignored, and so is a path a program assembles at run time, which no text search sees. Text alone cannot decide whether `$ROOT` or `~` is the project root, so every rule trades a missed caller against a wrong rewrite. A missed caller meets "not found" at its next run once the copy goes ([accept-list](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md) entry A3's kind of harm). A wrong rewrite points a line about some other file, such as a home script, at the suite's copy (entry A2's kind).

The state of play. Neither harm follows today: the built rule rewrites only certain references and holds the copy behind every uncertain one. Two gaps remain. A retired copy stays as long as an uncertain line names it, until the owner edits that line. A caller that builds the path in code goes unseen, and breaks once the copy goes. The sibling issue converge-repoints-observation-notes-and-migration-docs asks a neighboring question about which tracked files converge rewrites.

The ruling decides which references to a retired script converge repoints, which it leaves to the owner, and whether an uncertain one holds the retired copy.

recommendation.text:
Converge repoints a retired script reference only where its prefix names the project root with certainty, and counts as certain both the fixed root forms and any prefix it can prove resolves to the root, such as git's top-level idiom when the project root is the repository's top. A reference whose prefix may name the root but cannot be proven to stays as written: converge files an intake issue naming the line and keeps the retired copy, because that line still names it. A path built at run time is outside what converge can see, and its report says so when it removes a copy.

Rationale: this is option D, which keeps option A's guarantee and narrows its cost. The decision already says a caller whose behavior would change reaches the owner as an issue rather than as unrecorded work, and that the suite never edits human work beyond the retired-path exception; option B breaks the second by rewriting lines that may name another file, and option C breaks the first by letting a caller fail. Option A alone files an issue for a prefix converge could have settled, and the decision's rejected alternatives show the project wants no extra question on a migrated project's first converge where the answer is certain. The flip case: if projects whose root sits below their repository's top turn out to be common, the git idiom proves nothing in most of them, and option A alone is the simpler commitment.

title: Converge cannot tell whether a retired script path behind `$ROOT/`, `~/`, or `../` names the project's copy
